newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine minister makes discreet visit to London.
newsitem.headline: Argentine minister makes discreet visit to London.

text.p: Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella, under fire for policy on the disputed Falkland Islands, has made a surprise trip to London for talks with Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, officials said on Friday.

The Argentine foreign ministry and the British embassy in Buenos Aires both confirmed that Di Tella and Rifkind would be holding talks on Friday at Rifkind's official country residence, but they declined to give details of the agenda.
A spokesman for the Argentine Foreign Ministry said the government had tried to keep the visit quiet.

"We would have liked to handle this more discreetly, but it got out somehow without the Foreign Ministry's blessing," he said. Di Tella's deputy Andres Cisneros was likely to give some details of the visit later on Friday, the official said.

A British embassy spokesman described the meeting as informal talks on U.K.-Argentine relations and stressed: "No change to British sovereignty over the Falklands will be discussed. We are not offering or prepared to transfer or share sovereignty."

Argentina and Britain fought a brief but bloody war over the remote South Atlantic islands in 1982 in which about 1,000 soldiers, mostly Argentine, died. Argentina lost the war but maintains its claim to the islands, which it calls the Malvinas and says were "usurped" by Britain in 1833.

Britain keeps a garrison there and refuses to discuss sovereignty. But since Peronist President Carlos Menem came to power in 1989 he has resumed diplomatic ties, hosted visits by British royals and forged close trade links, while insisting he will win back the islands by the year 2000.

Di Tella has received flak for a charm offensive that has included sending islanders Christmas cards, books and videos. He recently admitted he has won little ground, then changed tack to claim he has secured a radical change in attitude among the islanders and managed to make the British nervous.
He also said a deal with Britain on oil exploration in the South Atlantic signed last year was "the biggest advance in 170 years" of territorial dispute.

Menem seemed to vent frustration at the lack of progress when he said in late December he would be willing to share sovereignty. But London immediately made it clear there was no question of shared rule.
